newsitem.title: USA: Aggressive U.S. antitrust stance, no 2nd bests.
newsitem.headline: Aggressive U.S. antitrust stance, no 2nd bests.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission's top merger litigator says the commission is moving away from accepting quick fixes, choosing instead to challenge flawed deals and permit others to go through.

"We're not in the horsetrading business, we are not in the business of compromise because 'something is better than nothing,' if we don't really believe it solves the problem," said George Cary in an interview Friday.
Cary was speaking generally, and not about specific actions of the FTC, such as the FTC's rejection Friday of a merger between Staples Inc. and Office Depot.
His comments were directed at what he sees as a gradual trend by the FTC. The Staples case is only the latest of many transactions in which the FTC has moved toward the new approach.
As Cary and others see it, the tendency of the FTC now is to require huge changes in flawed transactions or to reject them entirely.

This has coincided with new theories of competition to match changes in the economy. For example, a year ago, the FTC rejected the proposed merger of pharmacy chains Rite Aid and Revco, even though the merger would have preserved competition at the retail level.

Instead, the FTC focused on contracts between the emerging number of national health-care providers and large regional pharmacy chains. They reasoned that competition must be preserved between the chains of pharmacies that could negotiate such big contracts.
Rite Aid Corp. and Revco D.S. Inc. talked unsuccessfully with the FTC about restructuring their proposal.
Malcolm Pfunder, an attorney with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher in Washington, said the FTC approach reflected changes in the health industry and the way it related to pharmacies.
"They would not have pursued this five years ago because industry didn't work that way five years ago," he said, adding the FTC is "looking at competition as it now exists.:
Rite Aid and Revco also threatened to fight the FTC in court but then backed away from the expense of such complex litigation and abandoned the deal.
"The commission has been able to pursue this course because for the most part there has been no pushback," said Kevin Arquit, an attorney with Rogers & Wells in New York.
Arquit, who was once the top staff lawyer at the FTC, said he believes the trend will continue until a company successfully takes the commission to court.
"It will probably take a few court losses to reverse the trend," he said.
FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky, who is leading the commission in the new direction, knows the risk.

"It is very difficult for a plaintiff (either the government of a private party) to win" complex antitrust cases, he wrote nearly 15 years ago in the Georgetown Law Journal and last month said that still held true.
FTC chief merger litigator Cary also recognizes the risk of going to court but is standing firm.
"We're not blind to litigation risk, but if the proposed fix doesn't solve the problem that's not enough of a reason to accept the fix," said Cary.

That does not, however, preclude major changes to salvage deals if justified, he said. For example, the government required more than $1 billion in divestitures and licensing agreements to permit the creation of drug giant Novartis AG in December.
Steve Sunshine of Shearman and Sterling in Washington said he expected to see both the FTC and the antitrust division of the Justice Department become more aggressive.
He believes the tougher stance has come about because government lawyers have reviewed their cases and found past compromise agreements have in some cases been ineffective.
Staples and Office Depot had agreed to sell 63 stores from a total of more than 1,000 but the FTC said that even with the divestiture prices would have increased to consumers.
"They had a pretty good settlement on the table in the Staples case," he said. "They could have taken it with a fair amount of face."
